q: Which searching algorithm examines each item in turn, starting from the first?
ms: B — linear search checks the items one after another from the start.

q: Which algorithm **requires** the list to be sorted before it can be used?
ms: C — binary search relies on order to discard half the list at each step.

q: In a binary search, the first item examined is
options: the first item in the list
the last item in the list
the middle item of the list
ms: C — binary search always starts at the midpoint.

q: After each comparison, a binary search
options: halves the part of the list still being searched
ms: B — the half that cannot contain the target is discarded.

q: The **best case** for a binary search is when the target is
options: the first item in the list
the last item in the list
the middle item of the list
ms: D — the midpoint is examined first, so a target there is found in one comparison.

q: The **worst case** for a linear search on a list of n items needs
ms: C — if the target is last or absent, all n items are checked.

q: A sorted list holds 1,000 items. The **maximum** number of comparisons a binary search needs is about
ms: A — halving: 2¹⁰ = 1,024 > 1,000, so at most about 10 comparisons.

q: Which is an advantage of **linear** search over binary search?
options: It is faster on large lists
It halves the list each time
ms: B — linear search needs no preparation; binary requires sorted data.

q: A bubble sort works by repeatedly
options: comparing adjacent items and swapping them if needed
ms: B — neighbouring pairs are compared and swapped when out of order.

q: After the **first complete pass** of an ascending bubble sort, which is guaranteed?
options: The largest value is at the end
ms: C — the largest item bubbles to the end during pass 1.

q: A bubble sort knows the list is fully sorted when
options: the largest value reaches the end
a complete pass makes no swaps
ms: C — a swap-free pass proves every adjacent pair is in order.

q: One pass of a bubble sort over a list of 8 items makes
ms: B — n − 1 = 7 adjacent pairs are compared.

q: A merge sort begins by
options: repeatedly dividing the list in half
checking the midpoint against the target
ms: C — the list is split until each sub-list has one item.

q: In a merge sort, the dividing stops when
options: the largest item is at the end
ms: A — one-item lists are automatically sorted; merging then begins.

q: During the **merge** step, two sorted sub-lists are combined by
options: repeatedly taking the smaller of the two front items
ms: B — front items are compared and the smaller moves into the merged list.

q: Which sorting algorithm is generally the most efficient for a very large list?
ms: B — merge sort's divide-and-merge grows far more slowly than bubble sort's repeated passes. (Linear/binary are searches, not sorts.)

q: Which is an advantage of **bubble sort** over merge sort?
options: Simpler to implement and needs less memory
It works only on sorted lists
ms: B — bubble sort is simple and sorts in place; merge sort needs extra memory for merging.

q: A merge sort of 8 items requires how many **levels of dividing** (8 → 4 → 2 → 1)?
ms: B — three halvings: 8→4, 4→2, 2→1.

q: 1,000,000 sorted customer records are searched many times a day. The most suitable search is
options: linear search, because it is simpler
binary search, because it needs at most about 20 comparisons
bubble sort, because it swaps neighbours
either — they take the same time
ms: B — log₂(1,000,000) ≈ 20, versus up to 1,000,000 comparisons for linear.

q: A list is searched **once** and the data is unsorted. The best approach is
options: sort with merge sort, then binary search
ms: C — for a single search, sorting first costs more work than it saves.

q: Finding a word in a printed dictionary by opening the middle, deciding which half, and repeating is a real-world example of
ms: B — halving an ordered collection is exactly binary search.

q: Checking a pile of **unsorted** exam papers one by one for a particular name is an example of
ms: C — each item is examined in turn: linear search.

q: Which line correctly calculates the midpoint position in a binary search?
options: SET mid TO last DIV first
ms: A — the average of the two positions, using whole-number division.

q: In a binary search, the examined middle item is **less than** the target. What happens next?
ms: B — the target must be in the upper half, so the lower half (up to mid) is discarded.

q: A binary search ends with "not found" when
ms: A — the search area has shrunk to nothing.

q: In bubble sort pseudocode, the purpose of the variable `swapped` is to
options: record whether the current pass made any swaps
ms: B — if a pass finishes with swapped = FALSE, the sort stops.

q: Which sequence of values could a bubble sort's temp-swap use to exchange A = 9 and B = 4?
ms: A — save A in temp (9), copy B into A (4), copy temp into B (9).

q: Sorting a list into **descending** order with bubble sort means swapping a pair when
ms: B — for descending order, larger values move left, so swap when left < right.

q: A leaderboard of 500,000 scores must be re-sorted every minute. The most appropriate sort is
options: merge sort — efficient on large lists
binary search — it halves the list
ms: B — merge sort scales far better; the other two options are searches.

q: Which statement about merge sort is **false**?
options: It divides the list until single items remain
It merges sorted sub-lists in order
It requires extra memory during merging
It stops early if the list is already sorted
ms: D — standard merge sort performs all its divisions and merges regardless; it is bubble sort that can stop early after a swap-free pass.

q: A list of 16 sorted items is binary searched for a value that is **not present**. The number of comparisons made is about
ms: B — 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1: around log₂(16) = 4 comparisons (5 at most).

q: On **average**, a successful linear search of an n-item list examines about
ms: B — targets are equally likely anywhere, so on average half the list is checked.

q: Which task needs a **sort** rather than a search?
options: Finding whether "Priya" is on the register
Arranging race times from fastest to slowest
Checking if 42 is in a list
Finding the position of the word "cat"
ms: B — arranging items in order is sorting; the others locate an item.

q: Describe how a **linear search** finds a target value in a list. (3)
ms: Start at the first item (1); compare each item in turn with the target (1); stop when the target is found or the end of the list is reached (target not present) (1).

q: Describe how a **binary search** finds a target value in a sorted list. (4)
ms: Examine the middle item of the list (1); if it equals the target the search ends (1); otherwise discard the half that cannot contain the target (lower half if target is greater, upper half if smaller) (1); repeat on the remaining half until the target is found or no items remain (1).

q: Describe how a **merge sort** works. (4)
ms: Repeatedly divide the list in half (1) until each sub-list contains one item (1); then repeatedly merge pairs of sub-lists, comparing front items and taking the smaller first so each merged list is in order (1); continue merging until a single sorted list remains (1).

q: Describe how a **bubble sort** puts a list into ascending order. (3)
ms: Compare each pair of adjacent items, swapping them if they are in the wrong order, along the whole list (one pass) (1); repeat further passes (1); stop when a complete pass makes no swaps (1).

q: Give the **best case** and **worst case** for a binary search algorithm. (2)
ms: Best case: the target is the middle item, found on the first comparison (1). Worst case: the target is not in the list (or is only found when the search area shrinks to one item) (1).

q: Give the **best case** and **worst case** for a linear search algorithm. (2)
ms: Best case: the target is the first item — one comparison (1). Worst case: the target is the last item or not present — every item is checked (1).

q:
State why a binary search algorithm will **not** be appropriate for use with this sequence of numbers.

`55  33  2  47  89  14` (1)
ms: The sequence is not sorted/in order (1) — binary search only works on ordered data.

q: A data set of 100,000 customer IDs is stored in ascending order. State why a binary search algorithm would be preferable to a linear search algorithm for use with this data set. (1)
ms: It needs far fewer comparisons — it halves the search area each time (about 17 checks instead of up to 100,000), so it is much more efficient on this large sorted list (1).

q: Explain why a list **must** be sorted before a binary search can be used. (2)
ms: Binary search decides which half to discard by comparing the middle item with the target (1); if the data is unordered, the target could be in either half, so discarding a half might throw the target away (1).

q: Explain why the bubble sort is given the name **bubble**. (2)
ms: With each pass, the largest remaining value moves step by step to the end of the list (1) — values rise ('bubble up') to their correct position like bubbles rising in water (1).

q: A bubble sort is applied to a list of 12 items. State the number of comparisons made in **one** pass, and the number of items guaranteed to be in their final position after **two** complete passes. (2)
ms: One pass: 11 comparisons (n − 1) (1). After two passes the last two items (the two largest) are in their final positions (1).

q: State how a bubble sort determines that the list is fully sorted, and why this test is reliable. (2)
ms: It stops when a complete pass makes no swaps (1); no swaps means every adjacent pair is already in order, so the whole list must be sorted (1).

q: A sorted list contains 1,024 items. State the approximate **maximum** number of comparisons needed to find an item using (a) binary search and (b) linear search. (2)
ms: (a) about 10 (2¹⁰ = 1,024 — halve ten times) (1). (b) 1,024 — every item may need checking (1).

q: State **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of merge sort compared with bubble sort. (2)
ms: Advantage: much more efficient/faster on large lists (1). Disadvantage: more complex to implement / needs extra memory to hold the merged lists (1).

q: State **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of bubble sort compared with merge sort. (2)
ms: Advantage: simpler to implement / sorts in place with little extra memory / finishes in one pass on an already-sorted list (1). Disadvantage: very inefficient (many passes/comparisons) on large lists (1).

q:
A binary search examines the middle item of a sorted list and finds it is **greater than** the target.

State which half of the list is kept, and how the `last` position variable changes. (2)
ms: The lower half is kept — the target must be before the midpoint (1); last is set to mid − 1 (1).

q:
A linear search can be used on the list below but a binary search cannot be used **directly**.

`"Zara", "Adam", "Mia", "Ben"`

State what must be done first before a binary search could be used, and name an algorithm from this topic that could do it. (2)
ms: The list must be sorted into (alphabetical) order first (1); using a sorting algorithm such as merge sort (or bubble sort) (1).

q:
Complete the sentence.

A ______ search repeatedly examines the middle item of a sorted list and discards half the list each time. (1)
ms: binary (1).

q:
Complete the sentence.

A ______ search compares the target with each item in turn, starting at the beginning of the list. (1)
ms: linear (1).

q:
Complete the sentence.

A bubble sort compares ______ items and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. (1)
ms: adjacent / neighbouring (1).

q:
Complete the sentence.

A merge sort divides the list until each sub-list contains ______ item(s). (1)
ms: one (1).

q:
Complete the sentences.

After the first pass of an ascending bubble sort, the ______ value is in its final position at the ______ of the list. (2)
ms: largest (1); end (1).

q:
Complete the sentences.

In a binary search the midpoint is calculated as (first + last) ______ 2. The search reports 'not found' when first becomes ______ than last. (2)
ms: DIV (1); greater (1).

q:
Match each description to the correct algorithm (linear search, binary search, bubble sort, merge sort). One algorithm is not used.

**1** Divides the list into single items, then combines them in order
**2** Checks items one by one from the start
**3** Repeatedly halves the area being searched (3)
ms: 1 → merge sort (1); 2 → linear search (1); 3 → binary search (1). (Bubble sort unused.)

q:
Match each scenario to the most appropriate algorithm (linear search, binary search, bubble sort, merge sort). One algorithm is not used.

**1** Finding a ticket number in a huge, sorted list of ticket numbers
**2** Arranging 200,000 race finish times into order
**3** Checking a short, unsorted shopping list for "milk" (3)
ms: 1 → binary search (1); 2 → merge sort (1); 3 → linear search (1). (Bubble sort unused.)

q:
Match each phrase to bubble sort or merge sort.

**1** Needs extra memory while combining sub-lists
**2** Can finish after a single pass if the list is already in order
**3** Generally the better choice for very large lists (3)
ms: 1 → merge sort (1); 2 → bubble sort (1); 3 → merge sort (1).

q:
Complete the sentences.

The best case for a linear search is ______ comparison(s). The worst case for a linear search of n items is ______ comparison(s). (2)

A librarian keeps returned books in a random pile and finds titles by checking each one.

Name the search being performed, and state the change that would allow binary searching. (2)
ms: Linear search (1); the books would need to be sorted (e.g. alphabetically by title) first (1).

q: A contacts app stores names alphabetically. Explain why searching for a contact is fast even with 10,000 names. (2)
ms: Because the data is sorted, a binary search can be used (1); it halves the search area with each comparison, so about 14 comparisons at most are needed instead of up to 10,000 (1).

q: A student says: "Binary search is always better than linear search." Give **two** situations where this is not true. (2)
ms: Any two: the data is unsorted (binary cannot be used directly) (1); the list is very small, where linear is just as fast and simpler (1); the data is searched only once so sorting first isn't worth the cost (1).

q: A binary search is used on a sorted list of 15 items. State the position of the **first** item examined and the maximum number of items that remain in the search area after that first comparison. (2)
ms: Position 8 — the midpoint, (1+15) DIV 2 (1); at most 7 items remain (one half) (1).

q: An ascending bubble sort makes a pass in which **no** swaps occur, even though it is only the second pass. Explain what this means and what the algorithm does next. (2)
ms: Every adjacent pair is in order, so the list is already fully sorted (1); the algorithm stops — no further passes are needed (1).

q:
A bubble sort is used on a list of 5 items that is in **reverse** order (the worst case).

State (a) the number of comparisons in each pass, (b) the number of passes that make swaps, and (c) the total number of swaps performed. (3)
ms: (a) 4 comparisons per pass (n − 1) (1). (b) 4 passes make swaps (then a final checking pass makes none) (1). (c) 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10 swaps (1).

q:
During a merge sort, the sub-lists `[2, 7]` and `[3, 9]` are merged.

State the first comparison made and the first value placed into the merged list. (2)
ms: The front items 2 and 3 are compared (1); 2, the smaller, is placed first (1).

q: Explain why a one-item list needs no sorting, and why this fact matters in a merge sort. (2)
ms: A single item cannot be out of order with anything, so it is already sorted (1); merge sort divides until only one-item lists remain, guaranteeing every merge starts from sorted sub-lists (1).

q: A merge sort processes a list of 16 items. State the number of levels of **dividing** needed to reach single items, and the number of sub-lists after the **first** divide. (2)
ms: 4 levels (16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1) (1); 2 sub-lists of 8 after the first divide (1).

q: State the number of comparisons a binary search needs, at most, for sorted lists of (a) 64 items and (b) about 1,000,000 items. (2)
A linear search is used on a sorted list. Describe **one** improvement the sort order makes possible for unsuccessful searches. (2)
ms: The search can stop early as soon as an item larger than the target is reached (1) — the target cannot appear later in a sorted list, so the remaining items need not be checked (1).

q:
A shop's till searches a **sorted** product list of 30,000 barcodes for every item scanned, thousands of times per day.

State the appropriate search algorithm and justify your choice. (2)
ms: Binary search (1); the list is sorted and large and is searched repeatedly, so halving the search area (≈15 comparisons) is far more efficient than checking up to 30,000 items each scan (1).

q:
A quiz app shuffles its 20 questions into a random order, then must find one question by its text.

State the appropriate search algorithm and justify your choice. (2)
ms: Linear search (1); the data is unsorted (and small), so binary search cannot be used directly and sorting first is not worthwhile (1).

q:
A website search box looks up entered words in a sorted index of 2 million terms.

(a) State the appropriate search algorithm. (1)
(b) Estimate the maximum comparisons per lookup. (1)
(c) State the estimate for a linear search instead. (1)
ms: (a) Binary search (1). (b) About 21 (2²¹ ≈ 2 million) (1). (c) Up to 2,000,000 comparisons (1).

q: Explain why sorting a list **once** with merge sort can save time overall when the list will be searched **many** times. (2)
ms: After sorting, every search can use binary search with very few comparisons (1); the one-off cost of the sort is quickly repaid across many fast searches, compared with repeated slow linear searches (1).

q:
A fitness app records 10,000 run times in the order they happened, and shows a leaderboard sorted fastest-first.

Name a suitable algorithm for producing the leaderboard and justify the choice. (2)
ms: Merge sort (1); the list is large, so its divide-and-merge approach needs far fewer comparisons than bubble sort's repeated passes (1).

q:
A teacher sorts 6 test papers into mark order by hand, comparing neighbouring papers and swapping them.

Name the algorithm being mimicked and state why it is acceptable here despite its inefficiency. (2)
ms: Bubble sort (1); the list is tiny (6 items), so the number of comparisons is small and simplicity matters more than efficiency (1).

q: State the number of comparisons made when a linear search looks for a value that is in position 7 of a 20-item list, and the number made when the value is not in the list at all. (2)
ms: 7 comparisons (items 1 to 7) (1); 20 comparisons when absent — every item is checked (1).

q:
A binary search of a sorted 7-item list uses positions 1–7 and `mid = (first + last) DIV 2`.

State the sequence of **positions** examined when the target is at position 7. (3)
ms: Position 4 first (1); then first = 5, mid = (5+7) DIV 2 = 6 (1); then first = 7, mid = 7 — found. Sequence: 4, 6, 7 (1).

q: For the same 7-item list, state the sequence of positions examined when the target is at position 4, and the name given to this situation. (2)
ms: Position 4 only — found immediately (1); this is the best case (1).

q:
Two students search the same sorted 1,000-item list for the value at position 1. Student A uses linear search; Student B uses binary search.

State the number of comparisons each makes and who wins. (2)
ms: A: 1 comparison — the target is first (1). B: about 9–10 comparisons (midpoints down to position 1); Student A wins — linear's best case beats binary here (1).

q: Explain why bubble sort performs well when a list is **almost** sorted already. (2)
ms: Few adjacent pairs are out of order, so only a small number of swaps and passes are needed (1); it stops as soon as one pass has no swaps — possibly after just one or two passes (1).

q: State **two** pieces of information a trace of a bubble sort is usually expected to show in an exam answer. (2)
ms: Any two: the full list after each pass (1); the swaps/comparisons made (1); the pass on which no swaps occur (showing when it stops) (1).

q:
A binary search implementation sets `first TO mid` instead of `first TO mid + 1` when the target is greater than the middle item.

Explain the problem this causes when the search area shrinks to two items and the target is the second one. (3)
ms: mid = (first + last) DIV 2 equals first for a two-item area (1); since list(mid) < target, first is set to mid — i.e. unchanged (1); the search area never shrinks, so the loop repeats forever (infinite loop) (1).

q: State the purpose of the variable `temp` in a bubble sort swap, and what would happen without it. (2)
ms: It holds one value while the two items are exchanged (1); without it, the first assignment overwrites a value, so both positions end up holding the same item (1).

q:
A phone's music library of 40,000 songs is kept sorted by title. A new song is added occasionally; songs are searched constantly.

(a) Name the search used on the sorted titles. (1)
(b) Explain why keeping the library sorted at all times is worthwhile here. (2)
ms: (a) Binary search (1). (b) Searches vastly outnumber insertions (1); each search then needs only ≈16 comparisons instead of up to 40,000, so the small cost of inserting in order is repaid constantly (1).

q: Give **two** reasons why merge sort is preferred over bubble sort in professional software handling millions of records. (2)
ms: Far fewer comparisons/operations on large data — dramatically faster (1); its performance is consistent/predictable regardless of the initial order of the data (1).

q: A dataset is described as "sorted in descending order". A standard ascending binary search is run on it unchanged. Explain why it may fail to find values that are present. (2)
ms: The search assumes smaller values lie before the midpoint (1); with descending data the comparisons discard the half that actually contains the target, so it can be thrown away (1).

q:
An online dictionary must support: (i) finding a word instantly, (ii) adding new words each month, (iii) listing all words alphabetically.

State an appropriate algorithm for (i) and for producing (iii) after the monthly additions, and the property of the word list that (i) depends on. (3)
ms: (i) Binary search (1). (iii) Merge sort (accept bubble sort for a small update but merge preferred at scale) (1). Property: the word list must be kept in sorted (alphabetical) order (1).

q: State what is meant by the **efficiency** of a searching or sorting algorithm, and give the usual way it is measured in this topic. (2)
ms: How much work it takes to complete the task (1); measured by the number of comparisons (or passes/swaps) needed (1).

q:
A binary search of a sorted list uses positions 1–9.

State the position examined first, and the position examined second when the target is **greater** than the first item examined, and the position examined second when the target is **smaller**. (3)
ms: First: position 5 — (1+9) DIV 2 (1). Greater → first = 6, mid = (6+9) DIV 2 = 7 (1). Smaller → last = 4, mid = (1+4) DIV 2 = 2 (1).

q: A student traces a bubble sort but swaps items that are **equal**. State why this is unnecessary and the effect on the algorithm's stopping condition. (2)
ms: Equal items are already in an acceptable order, so swapping does nothing useful (1); counting such swaps makes passes appear to contain swaps, so the sort keeps making passes and may never register a swap-free pass correctly (1).

q: Explain why the number of comparisons a binary search needs grows only slowly as the list gets much bigger. (2)
ms: Each comparison halves the remaining search area (1); doubling the list size adds only one extra comparison (e.g. 1,000 → ~10, 2,000 → ~11) (1).

q:
A hospital system searches a sorted list of 500,000 patient IDs. A developer suggests switching from binary to linear search "to keep the code simpler".

Give a two-sided evaluation and a recommendation. (3)
ms: Linear is simpler to write and maintain (1); but it needs up to 500,000 comparisons per search versus about 19 for binary — far too slow at this scale/frequency (1); recommendation: keep binary search — the efficiency gain vastly outweighs the extra complexity (1).

q: State why the merge step of a merge sort always produces a sorted list, given the two sub-lists it merges. (2)
ms: Both sub-lists are themselves already in order (1); repeatedly taking the smaller front item means values enter the merged list in ascending order (1).

q:
An online game displays a leaderboard of 250,000 player scores, re-sorted after every match, and lets players search for any username in the sorted board.

Discuss which **sorting** and **searching** algorithms from this topic the game should use. (6)
ms: Level-marked. Sorting: merge sort — efficient and predictable on 250,000 items; bubble sort would need enormous numbers of passes/comparisons at this size, though it is simpler and could cope with an almost-sorted board after one match. Searching: binary search — the board is sorted, so each lookup needs ≈18 comparisons instead of up to 250,000 with linear; linear's only merits (works unsorted, simple) don't apply. Strong answers quantify comparisons, link choices to the sorted/large/repeated-use context, and give a clear recommendation. 5–6: both choices justified and applied with comparison; 3–4: correct choices with some justification; 1–2: identification only.

q:
A school stores 1,200 pupil records. Attendance staff look up pupils by surname all day; the office re-orders the whole list only once per term.

Discuss the searching approaches available and recommend one, referring to efficiency and any preparation the data needs. (6)
ms: Level-marked. Linear search: works on the list as-is, simple, but up to 1,200 comparisons per lookup, and lookups happen constantly. Binary search: needs the list kept in sorted order, but then ≈11 comparisons per lookup; sorting once per term (merge sort) is a tiny cost spread over thousands of lookups. Recommendation: sort the list and use binary search, as lookups vastly outnumber re-orderings. 5–6: both approaches evaluated with numbers and a justified recommendation including the sorting prerequisite; 3–4: sound comparison, limited quantification; 1–2: basic statements.

q: Compare bubble sort and merge sort on a list of just **5** items, and state which you would choose for this list. (3)
ms: On 5 items both finish almost instantly — efficiency differences are negligible (1); bubble sort is simpler to implement and uses no extra memory (1); choice: bubble sort (accept merge with justification), since simplicity outweighs speed at this size (1).

q:
A sensor logs one temperature per second into an unsorted file. Once per day, the day's 86,400 readings are sorted and the median found.

Name an appropriate sort, and explain why the sort makes finding values (such as the median or any given reading) easier. (3)
ms: Merge sort — large data set (1); once sorted, the median is simply the middle item, read directly (1); any value can then be located with a binary search in ≈17 comparisons (1).

q:
A student claims: "After three passes of an ascending bubble sort on any 8-item list, the last three items are sorted and no earlier item can ever be larger than them."

State whether each part of the claim is correct and justify your answers. (4)
ms: Part 1 correct: each pass fixes the next-largest value at the end, so after three passes the final three positions hold the three largest values in order (2). Part 2 correct: those are the three largest values in the whole list, so no earlier item can exceed them (2).
